one_liner: Low-delay HEVC/VVC encoder framework in C; README shows 2.4-4.7x x265 fast fps single-threaded, HEVC core binary-only.
what_it_does: Xin26x is one encoder framework for HEVC (h265_*), VVC (h266_*) and intra-only AV1 (h265p_*), aimed first at real-time communication and live streaming. It exposes its own plain C API: Xin26xEncoderCreate with an xin26x_params struct, Xin26xEncodeFrame per input frame (call with NULL to flush until bytesGenerate goes negative), Xin26xGetReconFrame, Xin26xControlOption for run-time IDR, frame-rate, bitrate, temporal-layer and rate-control changes, and Xin26xEncoderDelete; xin26x_test is the reference command-line client. It is not a drop-in for x265: different API, options and preset names, and the HEVC encoder and shared core ship only as prebuilt Windows static libraries.
how_it_is_fast: Not documented, and the HEVC encoder source is not in the repository, so the technique cannot be confirmed. The open option parser shows what the measured presets switch off: preset 0 (labelled 'superfast' in the CLI help) uses one reference frame, motion search mode 1, no RDOQ, no MCTF and no SMP, while preset 3 ('medium', used for BasketballDrive) raises references to 3 and turns MCTF on; a 48-frame lookahead and unit-tree (the cu-tree analogue) stay on by default. The README requires AVX2 and 2026 commits mention an 'intel optimized subroutine', so hand-vectorised kernels are likely part of it, but which kernels and how much they contribute is not visible.
when_to_use: Evaluating single-core, low-delay (IPPP, no B-frames) HEVC encoding on Windows x86-64 with AVX2, where the README shows 20.7-103.7 fps against 8.0-23.6 fps for x265 --preset fast at PSNR within 0.04 dB on natural 720p/1080p clips.

Screen-sharing style content in HEVC: the -s 1 mode turns on transform skip and 4x4 intra/inter partitions, and on sc_desktop it reached 40.08 dB against x265's 29.82 dB at the same 2 Mbit/s target (x265 ran without any screen-content tools).

Studying or extending an open VVC encoder: since June-July 2026 h266_core and h266_encoder build from source, and the offline table claims xin266 preset 6 at -41.5% BD-rate against x265 veryslow (no speed given).
Real-time pipelines that need run-time control of bitrate, frame rate, IDR insertion and temporal layers (up to 3) through Xin26xControlOption.
when_not_to_use: When the encoder must be auditable, rebuilt or run off Windows: h26x_core.lib, h265_core.lib and h265_enc.lib are prebuilt MSVC libraries, CMake's Linux and macOS branches look for .a files that do not exist (issue #12, 'cannot find -lxin26x', open since 2022), issue #15 (a Visual Studio build that 'does nothing') has been open since 2023, and the pre-built win64 encoder the README mentions is gone from testbin, which now holds only VvcDecoderApp.exe.

Non-x86 or pre-AVX2 CPUs: the README lists only Intel x86 with AVX2, ARM support (issue #11) has been open since 2021, and CMake's USE_INTRINSICS branch tests PROC_ARCH_ARM, which nothing sets, so even an ARM_PLATFORM build defines _X86_OPT_.

Closed-source or SaaS products: the LICENSE file is AGPL-3.0, 2026 source headers say GPL-3.0-or-later and the app files still say '(c) 2020, shennung ... All rights reserved', so the terms need clarifying before shipping.

Offline/VOD or multi-threaded encoding decisions: there are no multi-thread speed numbers, the offline table gives no speeds, and its fastest listed HEVC preset (xin265 p1) is 22.8% worse in BD-rate than x265 veryslow.
10-bit or non-4:2:0 sources, resolutions above the README's 3860x2160 limit, or more than 3 temporal layers; the sample client reads 8-bit 4:2:0 raw YUV only.

integration.form: static lib: HEVC encoder and shared core as prebuilt Windows .lib files; VVC, AV1-intra and API layers built from source with CMake
integration.dependencies: none external documented; the Windows client compiles the bundled third_party/getopt
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.5+ and Visual Studio 2022 (README); Windows release flags -W4 /arch:AVX -Oi -GL for the parts built from source
integration.platforms: Windows x86-64 with AVX2 in practice; Linux, macOS and ARM paths exist in CMakeLists.txt but the closed HEVC libraries exist only as .lib
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the API layer installs a process-wide logger (_XIN_LOGGER) from the first encoder created, so later encoders' pfXinLogEntry callbacks are ignored; otherwise each encoder has its own handle and internal thread pool (--thread)

gotchas: Xin26xEncoderReconfig is exported, but the API layer never assigns pfXinEncoderReconfig, so calling it jumps through a NULL function pointer. When Xin26xEncoderCreate fails (for example, a codec disabled at build time) it still returns a handle whose function pointers are NULL, so Xin26xEncoderDelete on it crashes and skipping it leaks.

The published low-delay commands omit the PSNR switches on both sides (xin26x's -P/--psnr leaves calcPsnr off by default; x265 needs --psnr, which --tune psnr does not set), and the achieved bitrates are not reported, so 'equal PSNR at equal ABR target' cannot be re-derived from the README commands.

Presets are not matched by name: xin26x preset 0 is its 'superfast' (preset 3 'medium' for BasketballDrive) against x265 --preset fast. The low-delay rows date from 28 Dec 2020 (README blame) and the HEVC .lib files have been replaced since ('update libs to fix bugs', Jul 2026), so the current binaries are not the ones measured.

-f means frame rate in xin26x_test but frame count in x265 (the BasketballDrive commands use -n 500 and -f 500 respectively); -r is rate-control mode, and the offline commands use -r 5, a value the CLI help (0-3) does not document.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Xin26x over Kvazaar only when single-core low-delay HEVC speed on Windows/AVX2 matters more than having source and portability, since Kvazaar is the open, cross-platform HEVC encoder in this category that also claims to beat x265. For VVC, VVenC has a published speed table against VTM; Xin26x's VVC encoder has quality claims only.
verified_claims_summary: README low-delay tables (added 28 Dec 2020), first-party, single thread, IPPP with ABR: xin26x 20.68 vs x265 7.96 fps on 1080p BasketballDrive (xin26x preset 3, 500 frames), 39.203 vs 8.35 on 1080p pedestrian_area, 103.68 vs 23.56 on 720p KristenAndSara (preset 0) and 39.48 vs 16.83 on 1080p sc_desktop (preset 0 plus screen-content mode, PSNR 40.08 vs 29.82 dB), i.e. 2.60x, 4.69x, 4.40x and 2.35x (derived from page data), against x265 --preset fast --tune psnr --pools 1 --no-wpp --frame-threads 0 --bframes 0. No CPU, compiler, flags, achieved bitrate or x265 version is given for these runs (the 2020/12/25 x265 build is named only for the offline table), FPS comes from different clients (xin26x_test divides frames by wall-clock time, including file I/O), and in current x265 source --pools 1 still creates a one-worker pool next to the frame-encoder thread, so neither run is strictly one core; CPU utilisation is not reported.
status_note: Single-author project, active (last commit 2026-08-26) and opening more source during 2026 (API in April, AV1-intra in May, VVC in June-July), but the HEVC encoder behind the speed table is still binary-only Windows libraries with conflicting licence headers, so treat it as an evaluation binary rather than a library to vendor.
